title: Rethinking Generative Image Pretraining: How Far Are We From Scaling Up Next-Pixel Prediction?
claim: Optimal scaling for raw-pixel modeling differs sharply from language and across target metrics, and scaling-law predictions match verified training runs.
layout: 4 line-plot panels in a row, shared FLOPs x-axis, red verification markers
description: A single row of four line plots, each with FLOPs on the x-axis in log scale. Panel (a) plots optimal tokens-per-parameter against FLOPs. Raw pixels (dark blue) fall from about 720 to 390. Language tokens (orange) stay flat near 20, far below the pixel curve. Panel (b) plots the same ratio for three metrics. Fréchet distance (green) sits highest at about 1200–1300 and rises slightly. Next-pixel loss (blue) and Top-1 accuracy (red) are lower and decline. Panel (c) shows Top-1 accuracy rising with FLOPs along a dashed blue line. A red triangle marks the measured point and nearly overlaps the final predicted point. Panel (d) shows Fréchet distance falling with FLOPs, with a red triangle for the real result next to the predicted point. Dashed lines with dots, grids, and serif titles. The eye goes first to the diverging curves in (a).
caption: Key findings on the scaling properties of next-pixel prediction, based on training Transformers on 32 × 32 images. (a) Learning on raw pixels (blue line) requires 10 −20× higher optimal token-to-parameter ratio than learning on language tokens (yellow line). (b) The optimal scaling strategy varies: generation-based completion quality (Fr´echet Distance, green) requires more training data optimally than classification (Top-1 accuracy, red) or the next-pixel prediction loss (blue). (c)-(d) The optimal-token and optimal-parameter setup is further verified by training models following the scaling prediction. Given 3.5e20 training FLOPs (with 5 × more compute), we project to reach 46.39% accuracy (vs. 46.41% in reality) and 244 Fr´echet Distance (vs. 240 Fr´echet Distance in reality).
abstract: This paper investigates the scaling properties of autoregressive next-pixel prediction, a simple, end-to-end yet under-explored framework for unified vision models. Starting with images at resolutions of 32x32, we train a family of Transformers using IsoFlops profiles across compute budgets up to 7e19 FLOPs and evaluate three distinct target metrics: next-pixel prediction objective, ImageNet classification accuracy, and generation-based completion measured by Fr'echet Distance. First, optimal scaling strategy is critically task-dependent. At a fixed resolution of 32x32 alone, the optimal scaling properties for image classification and image generation diverge, where generation optimal setup requires the data size grow three to five times faster than for the classification optimal setup. Second, as image resolution increases, the optimal scaling strategy indicates that the model size must grow much faster than data size. Surprisingly, by projecting our findings, we discover that the primary bottleneck is compute rather than the amount of training data. As compute continues to grow four to five times annually, we forecast the feasibility of pixel-by-pixel modeling of images within the next five years.
